leave it under the usual operations of set theory; an ``\textbf{axiom of
Universes}'' guarantees that every object lies in a Universe. For
details, see a book in preparation by C. Chevalley and the
speaker.\footnote{The eventual authors are C. Chevalley and P. Gabriel.
  The book is due out in the year 3000. Meanwhile, cf. also SGA 4 I.}
Thus the symbol \texttt{Set} denotes not the category of all sets, a
notion that has no sense, but the category of sets that lie in a given
Universe, which we shall not specify in the notation. Similarly,
\texttt{Cat} will denote the category of categories lying in the
Universe in question; the ``morphisms'' from one object \(X\) of
\texttt{Cat} to another \(Y\) are, by definition, the \textbf{functors}
from \(X\) to \(Y\).

If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a category, we denote by \(Ob(\mathcal{C})\)
\textbf{the set of objects} of \(\mathcal{C}\), and by
\(Fl(\mathcal{C})\) \textbf{the set of arrows} of \(\mathcal{C}\), or
morphisms of \(\mathcal{C}\). We shall therefore write \(X \in
Ob(\mathcal{C})\), avoiding the common abuse of notation
\(X \in \mathcal{C}\). If \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{C}'\) are two
categories, a \textbf{functor} from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{C}'\)
will always mean what is commonly called a \textbf{covariant} functor
from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{C}'\). Its data include both the
target category and the source category, \(\mathcal{C}\) and
\(\mathcal{C}'\). The functors from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{C}'\)
form a set, denoted \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}')\),
which is the set of objects of a category denoted \texttt{Hom̲(𝒞,𝒞′)}. By
definition, a \textbf{contravariant functor} from \(\mathcal{C}\) to
\(\mathcal{C}'\) is a functor from the \textbf{opposite category}
\(\mathcal{C}^{\circ}\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{C}'\).

We shall admit the notions of \textbf{projective limit} and
\textbf{inductive limit} of a functor \(F: \mathcal{I} \to
\mathcal{C}\), and in particular the most common special cases of these
notions: cartesian products and fiber products, the dual notions of
direct sums and amalgamated sums, and the usual formal properties of
these operations.

For example, in the category \texttt{Cat} introduced above, projective
limits, relative to categories \(\mathcal{I}\) lying in the chosen
Universe, exist. The set of objects, respectively the set of arrows, of
the projective-limit category \(\mathcal{C}\) of the \(\mathcal{C}_{i}\)
is obtained by taking the projective limit of the sets of objects,
respectively the sets of arrows, of the categories \(\mathcal{C}_{i}\).
The best-known case is that of the product of a family of categories. We
shall constantly use, in what follows, the fiber product of two
categories over a third.

For everything concerning categories and functors, pending the book in
preparation already mentioned, see {[}VI.1{]}, which is necessarily
quite incomplete, even as concerns the generalities sketched in the
present number.

Let us take this occasion to spell out the notion of equivalence of
categories, which is not presented satisfactorily in {[}VI.1{]}. A
functor \(F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}'\) is said to be
\textbf{faithful}, respectively \textbf{fully faithful}, if for every
pair of objects \(S\), \(T\) of \(\mathcal{C}\), the map
\(u \mapsto F(u)\) from \(\operatorname{Hom}(S,T)\) to
\(\operatorname{Hom}(F(S),F(T))\) is injective, respectively bijective.
One says that \(F\) is an \textbf{equivalence} of categories if

\(F\) is fully faithful and, moreover, every object \(S'\) of
\(\mathcal{C}'\) is isomorphic to an object of the form \(F(S)\). One
shows that this is the same as saying that there exists a functor \(G\)
from \(\mathcal{C}'\) to \(\mathcal{C}\) \textbf{quasi-inverse} to
\(F\), i.e.~such that \texttt{GF} is isomorphic to \(id_{\mathcal{C}}\)
and \texttt{FG} is isomorphic to \(id_{\mathcal{C}}'\).

When this is so, giving a functor \(G: \mathcal{C}' \to \mathcal{C}\)
and an isomorphism \(\phi: FG \to id_{\mathcal{C}}'\) is equivalent to
giving, for every \(S' \in Ob(\mathcal{C}')\), a pair \((S,u)\) formed
by an object \(S\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) and an isomorphism
\(u: F(S) \to S'\), namely \((G(S'), \phi(S'))\). With this notation,
there exists a unique functor \(\mathcal{C}' \to \mathcal{C}\) having
the given map \(S' \mapsto G(S')\) as its object map, and such that the
map \(S'
\mapsto \phi(S')\) is a homomorphism of functors
\(FG \to id_{\mathcal{C}}'\).

Finally, if \(G\) is a functor quasi-inverse to \(F\), and if one
chooses isomorphisms \(\phi: FG \simeq id_{\mathcal{C}}'\) and
\(\psi: GF \simeq id_{\mathcal{C}}\), then the two compatibility
conditions on \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) stated in {[}VI.1, I.1.2{]} are in
fact equivalent to one another; and for every chosen isomorphism
\(\phi\), there exists a unique isomorphism \(\psi\) such that those
conditions are satisfied.

\section{2. Categories over Another
Category}\label{categories-over-another-category}

Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a category in the chosen Universe. It is
therefore an object of \texttt{Cat}, and one may consider the category
\(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\) of ``objects of \texttt{Cat} over
\(\mathcal{E}\)''. An object of this category is therefore a functor

\[ p: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{E}. \]

One also says that the category \(\mathcal{F}\), endowed with such a
functor, is a \textbf{category over} \(\mathcal{E}\), or an
\textbf{\(\mathcal{E}\)-category}. Thus an
\textbf{\(\mathcal{E}\)-functor} from a category \(\mathcal{F}\) over
\(\mathcal{E}\) to a category \(\mathcal{G}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) will
mean a functor

\[ f: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G} \]

such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{qf = p,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(p\) and \(q\) are the projection functors for \(\mathcal{F}\)
and \(\mathcal{G}\) respectively. The set of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors
\(f\) from \(\mathcal{F}\) to \(\mathcal{G}\) is therefore in bijective
correspondence with the set of arrows with source \(\mathcal{F}\) and
target \(\mathcal{G}\) in \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\),

without this being an identity, since the data of an \(f\) as above does
not determine \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) as categories over
\(\mathcal{E}\). Of course, as in any other category
\(\mathcal{C}_{/}S\), we shall routinely make the abuse of language that
identifies \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors, in the sense just explained, with
arrows in a category \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\).

We shall denote by

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}) \]

the set of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors from \(\mathcal{F}\) to
\(\mathcal{G}\). Of course, a composite of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors is
an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor, the composition in question corresponding by
definition to the composition of arrows in \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\).

Now consider two \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors

\[ f,g: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G} \]

and a homomorphism of functors

\[ u: f \to g. \]

One says that \(u\) is an \textbf{\(\mathcal{E}\)-homomorphism}, or a
``\textbf{homomorphism of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors}'', if for every
\(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{F})\), one has

\[ q(u(\xi)) = id_{p(\xi)}. \]

In words: putting
\(S = p(\xi) = qf(\xi) = qg(\xi) \in Ob(\mathcal{E})\), the morphism

\[ u(\xi): f(\xi) \to g(\xi) \]

in \(\mathcal{G}\) is an \(id_{S}\)-morphism. In general, for every
morphism \(\alpha: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\) and every category
\(\mathcal{G}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), a morphism \(v\) in
\(\mathcal{G}\) is called an \textbf{\(\alpha\)-morphism} if \(q(v) =
\alpha\), where \(q\) denotes the projection functor
\(\mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{E}\). If one has a third
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functor \(h: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) and an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-homomorphism \(v: g \to h\), then \texttt{vu} is again
an \(\mathcal{E}\)-homomorphism.

Thus \textbf{the \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors from \(\mathcal{F}\) to
\(\mathcal{G}\), and the \(\mathcal{E}\)-homomorphisms between them,
form a subcategory of the category \texttt{Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢)} of all functors
from \(\mathcal{F}\) to \(\mathcal{G}\); it will be called the category
of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors from \(\mathcal{F}\) to \(\mathcal{G}\) and
denoted}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is also the kernel subcategory of the pair of functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R,S: Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢) ⇉ Hom̲(ℱ,ℰ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(R\) is the constant functor defined by the object \(p\) of
\texttt{Hom̲(ℱ,ℰ)}, and \(S\) is the functor \(f \mapsto q \circ f\)
defined by \(q: \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{E}\).

To finish these generalities, it remains to define the natural pairings
between the categories \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)} by composition of
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors. In other words, one wants to define a
``composition functor''

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(i)  Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢) × Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(𝒢,ℋ) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,ℋ)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

when \(\mathcal{F}\), \(\mathcal{G}\), \(\mathcal{H}\) are three
categories over \(\mathcal{E}\), in such a way that this functor
induces, on objects, the composition map \((f,g) \mapsto gf\) for
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors \(f: \mathcal{F} \to
\mathcal{G}\) and \(g: \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{H}\). For this, recall
that one defines a canonical functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(ii) Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢) × Hom̲(𝒢,ℋ) → Hom̲(ℱ,ℋ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which on objects is just the composition map \((f,g) \mapsto gf\) of
functors, and which transforms an arrow \((u,v)\), where

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u: f → f′,    v: g → g′,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are arrows in \texttt{Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢)}, respectively in \texttt{Hom̲(𝒢,ℋ)}, into
the arrow

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{v ∗ u: gf → g′f′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined by the relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(v ∗ u)(ξ) = v(f′(ξ)) · g(u(ξ)) = g′(u(ξ)) · v(f(ξ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is well known that one indeed obtains in this way a homomorphism from
\texttt{gf} to \(g'f'\), and that, for variable \(f\), \(g\) and \(u\),
\(v\), one obtains the functor (ii); that is, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(I)   id\_g ∗ id\_f = id\_\{gf\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(II)  (v′ ∗ u′) ∘ (v ∗ u) = (v′ ∘ v) ∗ (u′ ∘ u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Recall also that one has an associativity formula for the canonical
pairings (ii), expressed on the one hand by the associativity
\((hg)f = h(gf)\) of the composition of functors, and on the other hand
by the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(III) (w ∗ v) ∗ u = w ∗ (v ∗ u)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for the composition products of homomorphisms of functors, where
\(u: f \to f'\) and \(v: g \to g'\) are as above, and where one supposes
given in addition a homomorphism \(w: h \to h'\) of functors
\(h,h': \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{K}\).

I now say that \textbf{when \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are
\(\mathcal{E}\)-categories, the canonical composition functor (ii)
induces a functor (i)}. Since we already know that the composite of two
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors is an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor, this amounts to
saying that \textbf{when \(u: f \to f'\) and \(v: g \to g'\) are
homomorphisms of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors, then
\(v \ast u: gf \to g'f'\) is also a homomorphism of
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors}. This follows trivially from the definitions.
Since the pairings (i) are induced by the pairings (ii), they satisfy
the same associativity property, also expressed in the formulas
\((hg)f = h(gf)\) and \((w \ast v) \ast u = w \ast (v \ast u)\), for
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors and \(\mathcal{E}\)-homomorphisms of
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors.

To complete the formulary (I), (II), (III), recall also the formulas

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(IV)  v ∗ id\_ℱ = v    and    id\_𝒢 ∗ u = u,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where, for simplicity, one writes \(v \ast f\) or \(u \ast g\) instead
of \(v \ast u\) when \(u\), respectively \(v\), is the identity
automorphism of \(f\), respectively \(g\).

It follows from the definition of the pairings (i) that
\textbf{\texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)} is a functor in \(\mathcal{F}\) and
\(\mathcal{G}\), from the product category
\(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}^{\circ} \times Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\) to the category
\texttt{Cat}}. Indeed, if \(g: \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{G}_{1}\) is an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functor, i.e.~an object of \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(𝒢,𝒢₁)},
then by taking \(\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{G}_{1}\) in (i), there
corresponds to it a functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_*: Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢₁).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One defines analogously, for an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
\(f: \mathcal{F}_{1} \to \mathcal{F}\), a functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\^{}*: Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ₁,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For short, these functors are also denoted by the symbols
\(f \mapsto g \circ f\) and \(g \mapsto g \circ f\) respectively; these
in fact denote only the corresponding maps on the sets of objects. It
follows from the associativity property indicated above that one does
indeed obtain in this way, as announced, a functor
\texttt{Cat\_/ℰ°\ ×\ Cat\_/ℰ\ →\ Cat}.

\section{3. Base Change in Categories over
ℰ}\label{base-change-in-categories-over-ux2130}

Since projective limits exist in \texttt{Cat}, relative to categories
\(\mathcal{I}\) belonging to the Universe, the same is true in
\(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\). In particular, cartesian products exist there;
these are interpreted as fiber products in \texttt{Cat}. In accordance
with the general notation, if \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) are
categories over \(\mathcal{E}\), we denote by

\[ \mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{G} \]

their product in \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\), i.e.~their fiber product over
\(\mathcal{E}\) in \texttt{Cat}, regarded as a category over
\(\mathcal{E}\). Thus \(\mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{G}\)
is endowed with two \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors \(pr_{1}\) and \(pr_{2}\),
which define, for every category \(\mathcal{H}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), a
bijection

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_ℰ(ℋ, ℱ ×\_ℰ 𝒢) ≃ Hom\_ℰ(ℋ,ℱ) × Hom\_ℰ(ℋ,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This bijection moreover comes from an isomorphism of categories

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℋ, ℱ ×\_ℰ 𝒢) ≃ Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℋ,ℱ) × Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℋ,𝒢),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by taking the sets of objects of the two sides. The displayed functor is
the one whose components are the functors \(h
\mapsto pr_{1} \circ h\) and \(h \mapsto pr_{2} \circ h\) from the first
member to the two factors of the second. We leave to the reader the
verification that one indeed obtains an isomorphism in this way; the
analogous fact is true more generally whenever one has a projective
limit of categories, and not only in the case of a fiber product.

Recall moreover, as was said in VI.1, that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ob(ℱ ×\_ℰ 𝒢) = Ob(ℱ) ×\_\{Ob(ℰ)\} Ob(𝒢),}
\NormalTok{Fl(ℱ ×\_ℰ 𝒢) = Fl(ℱ) ×\_\{Fl(ℰ)\} Fl(𝒢),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the composition of arrows being carried out componentwise.

In what follows, we consider a functor

\[ \lambda: \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E}, \]

and, for every category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), we regard
\(\mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}'\) as a category over
\(\mathcal{E}'\) by means of \(pr_{2}\). In other words, we interpret
the ``fiber product'' operation as an operation of \textbf{``base
change''}, the functor \(\lambda: \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E}\) being
called the \textbf{``base-change functor.''} In accordance with the
well-known general facts, one obtains in this way a functor, called the
\textbf{base-change functor} for \(\lambda\):

\[ \lambda*: Cat_{/}\mathcal{E} \to Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}'. \]

It is adjoint to the ``restriction of the base'' functor, which sends
every category \(\mathcal{F}'\) over \(\mathcal{E}'\), with projection
functor \(p'\), to \(\mathcal{F}'\) regarded as a category over
\(\mathcal{E}\) by the functor \(p = \lambda
p'\). As is well known for a base-change functor in a category, the
base-change functor ``commutes with projective limits'', and in
particular ``transforms'' fiber products over \(\mathcal{E}\) into fiber
products over \(\mathcal{E}'\).

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) be two categories over
\(\mathcal{E}\). We shall define a \textbf{canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(i)  Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ′,𝒢′) ≃ Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′,𝒢),}
\NormalTok{     where ℱ′ = ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′ and 𝒢′ = 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For this, consider the functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr₁: 𝒢′ = 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′ → 𝒢,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and define (i) by

\[ F \mapsto pr_{1} \circ F, \]

which a priori denotes a functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(ii) Hom̲(ℱ′,𝒢′) → Hom̲(ℱ′,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It remains only to verify that this latter functor induces a functor on
the subcategories in (i), and that this induced functor is an
isomorphism. That (ii) induces a bijection

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ′,𝒢′) ≃ Hom\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′,𝒢)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is the characteristic property of the base-change functor. It remains
therefore

to prove that if \(F\), \(G\) are \(\mathcal{E}'\)-functors
\(\mathcal{F}' \to \mathcal{G}'\), then \textbf{the map}

\[ u \mapsto pr_{1} \circ u \]

\textbf{induces a bijection}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{ℰ′\}(F,G) ≃ Hom\_ℰ(pr₁ ∘ F, pr₁ ∘ G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The verification of this fact is immediate and is left to the reader.

It follows from this isomorphism (i), and from the end of the preceding
number, that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′, 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{may be regarded as a functor in \(\mathcal{E}'\),
\(\mathcal{F}\), \(\mathcal{G}\), from the category
\texttt{Cat\_/ℰ°\ ×\ Cat\_/ℰ°\ ×\ Cat\_/ℰ} to the category
\texttt{Cat}}, isomorphic to the functor defined by the expression

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, for fixed \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\), one
obtains a functor in \(\mathcal{E}'\). Thus the \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
of projection \(\lambda: \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E}\) defines a
morphism, i.e.~a functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{λ*\_\{ℱ,𝒢\}: Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ′,𝒢′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which we now spell out. On the sets of objects of the two sides, it is
the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ↦ f′ = f ×\_ℰ ℰ′,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

expressing the functorial dependence of
\(\mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}'\) on the object
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\). On the other hand, consider two
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors

\[ f,g: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G} \]

and a homomorphism of \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors

\[ u: f \to g. \]

We shall spell out the corresponding homomorphism of
\(\mathcal{E}'\)-functors

\[ u': f' \to g'. \]

For every

\[ \xi' = (\xi,S') \in Ob(\mathcal{F}') \]

with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ξ ∈ Ob(ℱ),    S′ ∈ Ob(ℰ′),    p(ξ) = λ(S′) = S,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u′(ξ′): f′(ξ′) = (f(ξ),S′) → g′(ξ′) = (g(ξ),S′)    in 𝒢′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is defined by the formula

\[ u'(\xi') = (u(\xi), id_{S'}). \]

This is indeed an \(S'\)-morphism in \(\mathcal{G}'\), since
\(q(u(\xi)) = \lambda(id_{S'}) = id_{S}\).

Now consider any \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor

\[ \lambda': \mathcal{E}'' \to \mathcal{E}' \]

and the corresponding functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′, 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′)}
\NormalTok{  → Hom̲\_\{ℰ″/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ″, 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ″).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

I say that this functor is none other than the one obtained by the
preceding process, starting from \(\mathcal{F}'\) and \(\mathcal{G}'\)
over \(\mathcal{E}'\) and regarding \(\mathcal{E}''\) as a category over
\(\mathcal{E}'\), taking into account the isomorphisms of
\textbf{``transitivity of base change''}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℱ′ ×\_ℰ′ ℰ″ ≃ ℱ″ = ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ″,}
\NormalTok{𝒢′ ×\_ℰ′ ℰ″ ≃ 𝒢″ = 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ″,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which imply a canonical isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ″/{-}\}(ℱ′ ×\_ℰ′ ℰ″, 𝒢′ ×\_ℰ′ ℰ″)}
\NormalTok{  ≃ Hom̲\_\{ℰ″/{-}\}(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ″, 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ″).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The verification of this compatibility is immediate and is left to the
reader.

The functors just defined are compatible with the pairings defined in
the preceding number. More precisely, if \(\mathcal{F}\),
\(\mathcal{G}\), \(\mathcal{H}\) are categories over \(\mathcal{E}\) and
if one puts

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℱ′ = ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′,    𝒢′ = 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′,    ℋ′ = ℋ ×\_ℰ ℰ′,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one has commutativity in the following diagram of functors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢) × Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(𝒢,ℋ)  →  Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,ℋ)}
\NormalTok{        ↓ λ*\_\{ℱ,𝒢\} × λ*\_\{𝒢,ℋ\}              ↓ λ*\_\{ℱ,ℋ\}}
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ′,𝒢′) × Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(𝒢′,ℋ′) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ′/{-}\}(ℱ′,ℋ′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the horizontal arrows are the composition functors defined in the
preceding number. This commutativity is expressed by the formulas

\[ (gf)' = g'f' \]

for \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})\),
\(g \in
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{H})\), a formula
which simply expresses the functoriality of base change, and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(v ∗ u)′ = v′ ∗ u′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

when \(u: f \to f_{1}\) is an arrow of \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)} and
\(v: g \to g_{1}\) is an arrow of \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(𝒢,ℋ)}. The
verification of this formula follows easily from the definitions.

In what follows, we shall be chiefly interested in \texttt{Hom̲\_ℰ(ℱ,𝒢)},
and certain remarkable subcategories of it, when
\(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{E}\). For this reason we introduce a special
notation:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ̲(𝒢/ℰ) = Hom̲\_ℰ(ℰ,𝒢),}
\NormalTok{Γ(𝒢/ℰ) = Ob(Γ̲(𝒢/ℰ)) = Hom\_ℰ(ℰ,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remarks.} When \(\mathcal{E}\) is a point category,
i.e.~\(Ob(\mathcal{E})\) and \(Fl(\mathcal{E})\) are reduced to a single
element, which also means that \(\mathcal{E}\) is a final object of the
category \texttt{Cat}, then the data of a category over \(\mathcal{E}\)
is equivalent to the data of a category in the ordinary sense, since
there will be a unique functor from \(\mathcal{F}\) to \(\mathcal{E}\).
More precisely, \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\) is then isomorphic to
\texttt{Cat}. Moreover, the categories \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)} are
then none other than the \texttt{Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢)}.

Recall then that the fundamental formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(ℋ, Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢)) ≃ Hom(ℱ × ℋ, 𝒢),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

functorial in the three arguments appearing in it, allows
\texttt{Hom̲(ℱ,𝒢)} to be interpreted axiomatically, in terms internal to
the category \texttt{Cat}. Thus the familiar formulary for
\texttt{Hom̲}-categories appears as a special case of a formulary valid
in categories such as \texttt{Cat}, where ``\texttt{Hom̲}-objects'',
defined by the preceding formula, exist. There is an analogous
interpretation of \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)}, when \(\mathcal{E}\) is
again arbitrary, by the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(ℋ, Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,𝒢)) ≃ Hom\_ℰ(ℱ × ℋ, 𝒢),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

functorial in the three arguments. In this way, the formal properties
set out in VI.2 and VI.3 are special cases of more general results,
valid in categories where the objects \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)}, for
\(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) two objects of the category over a
third object \(\mathcal{E}\), exist.

\section{4. Fiber Categories; Equivalence of
ℰ-Categories}\label{fiber-categories-equivalence-of-ux2130-categories}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{E}\), and let
\(S \in Ob(\mathcal{E})\). The \textbf{fiber category} of
\(\mathcal{F}\) at \(S\) is the subcategory \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) of
\(\mathcal{F}\) that is the inverse image of the point subcategory of
\(\mathcal{E}\) defined by \(S\).

Thus the objects of \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) are the objects \(\xi\) of
\(\mathcal{F}\) such that \(p(\xi) = S\), and its morphisms are the
morphisms \(u\) of \(\mathcal{F}\) such that \(p(u) = id_{S}\), i.e.~the
\(S\)-morphisms in \(\mathcal{F}\). Of course, \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) is
canonically isomorphic to the fiber product
\(\mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} {S}\), where \({S}\) denotes the
point subcategory of \(\mathcal{E}\) defined by \(S\), endowed with its
inclusion functor into \(\mathcal{E}\). It follows, taking the
transitivity of base change into account, that if one makes a base
change \(\lambda: \mathcal{E}' \to
\mathcal{E}\), then for every \(S' \in Ob(\mathcal{E}')\), \textbf{the
projection \(pr_{1}: \mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{F}
\times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{F}\) induces an
isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℱ′\_\{S′\} → ℱ\_S,    where S = λ(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(f: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) be an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor. If
\(f\) is fully faithful, then for every base change
\(\mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E}\), the corresponding functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f′: ℱ′ = ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′ → 𝒢′ = 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is fully faithful.

The verification is immediate. More generally, one can show that every
projective limit of fully faithful functors, here \(f\) and the identity
functors in \(\mathcal{E}\) and \(\mathcal{E}'\), is a fully faithful
functor.

One should note that the assertion analogous to 4.1, with ``fully
faithful'' replaced by ``equivalence of categories'', is false, already
for \(\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{E}\). However:

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(f: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) be an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor.
The following conditions are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  There exists an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
  \(g: \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{E}\)-isomorphisms
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gf ≃ id\_ℱ,    fg ≃ id\_𝒢.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  For every category \(\mathcal{E}'\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), the functor
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f′ = f ×\_ℰ ℰ′: ℱ′ = ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′ → 𝒢′ = 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an equivalence of categories.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \(f\) is an equivalence of categories, and for every
  \(S \in Ob(\mathcal{E})\), the functor \(f_{S}: \mathcal{F}_{S} \to
  \mathcal{G}_{S}\) induced by \(f\) is an equivalence of categories.
\item
  \(f\) is fully faithful, and for every \(S \in Ob(\mathcal{E})\) and
  every \(\eta \in Ob(\mathcal{G}_{S})\), there exist
  \(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{S})\) and an \(S\)-isomorphism
  \(u: f(\xi) \to \eta\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} Evidently (1) implies that \(f\) is an equivalence of
categories, a notion defined by the same condition but without requiring
the isomorphisms of functors to be \(\mathcal{E}\)-morphisms. On the
other hand, it follows from the functorialities of the preceding number
that condition (1) is preserved after base change \(\mathcal{E}' \to
\mathcal{E}\). Hence (1) ⇒ (2). Evidently (2) ⇒ (3), since it is enough
to take \(\mathcal{E}' = \mathcal{E}\) and \(\mathcal{E}' = {S}\). It is
still more trivial that (3) ⇒ (4). It remains to prove (4) ⇒ (1).

For this, choose for every \(\eta \in Ob(\mathcal{G})\) an object
\(g(\eta) \in Ob(\mathcal{F})\) and an isomorphism
\(u(\eta): f(g(\eta)) \to \eta\) such that \(q(u(\eta)) = id_{S}\),
where \(S = q(\eta)\). This is possible by the second condition in (4).
As is known and immediate, the fact that \(f\) is fully faithful implies
that \(g\) can be regarded in a unique way as a functor from
\(\mathcal{G}\) to \(\mathcal{F}\), so that the \(u(\eta)\) define a
functorial homomorphism, hence isomorphism,

\[ u: fg \simeq id_{\mathcal{G}}. \]

Moreover, by construction, \(g\) is an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor and \(u\)
an \(\mathcal{E}\)-homomorphism. To the preceding data there then
corresponds a functorial isomorphism \(v: gf \to id_{\mathcal{F}}\),
defined by the condition \(f \ast v = u
\ast f\), and one sees at once that it is also an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-morphism. This proves the assertion.

\textbf{Definition.}

If the preceding conditions are satisfied, one says that \(f\) is an
\textbf{equivalence of categories over \(\mathcal{E}\)}, or an
\textbf{\(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence}.

\textbf{Corollary.}

Suppose that the projection functor \(p: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{E}\)
is a transportable functor, i.e.~that for every isomorphism
\(\alpha: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\) and every object \(\xi\) in
\(\mathcal{F}_{T}\), there exists an isomorphism \(u\) in
\(\mathcal{F}\) with source \(\xi\) such that \(p(u) = \alpha\). Then
every \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor \(f: \mathcal{F} \to
\mathcal{G}\) that is an equivalence of categories is an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence.

This follows

from criterion (4).

\textbf{Corollary.}

Let \(f: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) be an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence. Then for every category \(\mathcal{H}\)
over \(\mathcal{E}\), the corresponding functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(𝒢,ℋ) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℱ,ℋ),}
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℋ,ℱ) → Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℋ,𝒢)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are equivalences of categories.

This follows from criterion (1) by the usual argument.

\section{5. Cartesian Morphisms, Inverse Images, Cartesian
Functors}\label{cartesian-morphisms-inverse-images-cartesian-functors}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{E}\), with projection
functor \(p\).

\textbf{Definition.}

Consider a morphism

\[ \alpha: \eta \to \xi \]

in \(\mathcal{F}\), and let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S = p(ξ),    T = p(η),    f = p(α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One says that \(\alpha\) is a \textbf{cartesian morphism} if, for every
\(\eta' \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{T})\) and every \(f\)-morphism
\(u: \eta' \to \xi\), there exists a unique \(T\)-morphism
\(\bar{u}: \eta' \to \eta\) such that \(u = \alpha \circ \bar{u}\).

This therefore means that, for every \(\eta' \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{T})\),
the map \(v \mapsto \alpha \circ v\)

\[ (i) \operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta',\eta) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta',\xi) \]

is bijective. It also means that the pair \((\eta,\alpha)\)
\textbf{represents, as a functor in \(\eta'\)}, the functor
\(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}_{T} \to Set\) given by the second member.

If, for a given morphism \(f: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\) and a given
\(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{S})\), such a pair \((\eta,\alpha)\) exists,
i.e.~a cartesian morphism \(\alpha\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) with target
\(\xi\) and with \(p(\alpha) = f\), then \(\eta\) is determined in
\(\mathcal{F}_{T}\) up to unique isomorphism. One then says that
\textbf{the inverse image of \(\xi\) by \(f\) exists}, and an object
\(\eta\) of \(\mathcal{F}_{T}\) endowed with a cartesian \(f\)-morphism
\(\alpha: \eta \to \xi\) is called \textbf{an inverse image of \(\xi\)
by \(f\)}.

Often, once \(\mathcal{F}\) is fixed, one assumes such an inverse image
chosen whenever it exists. The inverse image will then be denoted by
symbols such as \(f*_{\mathcal{F}}(\xi)\), or simply \(f*(\xi)\), or
\(\xi \times_{S} T\) when these notations cause no confusion. In what
follows, the canonical morphism \(\alpha: \eta \to \xi\) will then be
denoted \(\alpha_{f}(\xi)\).

If for every \(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{S})\) the inverse image of
\(\xi\) by \(f\) exists, one also says that \textbf{the inverse-image
functor by \(f\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) exists}, and \(f*(\xi)\) then
becomes a \textbf{covariant functor in \(\xi\)}, from
\(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) to \(\mathcal{F}_{T}\). This comes from the fact
that the second member in (i) depends covariantly on \(\xi\), or more
precisely denotes a functor from
\(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}_{T} \times \mathcal{F}_{S}\) to \texttt{Set}.

This functorial dependence of \(f*(\xi)\) is made explicit as follows.
Consider cartesian \(f\)-morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α: η → ξ,    α′: η′ → ξ′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and an \(S\)-morphism \(\lambda: \xi \to \xi'\). Then there exists a
unique \(T\)-morphism \(\mu: \eta \to \eta'\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α′ μ = λ α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

as follows from the fact that \(\alpha'\) is cartesian.

Also note the following immediate fact. Consider a commutative diagram
in \(\mathcal{F}\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{η  {-}{-}α{-}{-}\textgreater{}  ξ}
\NormalTok{|         |}
\NormalTok{μ         λ}
\NormalTok{↓         ↓}
\NormalTok{η′ {-}{-}α′{-}\textgreater{} ξ′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha'\) are \(f\)-morphisms, \(\lambda\) is an
\(S\)-isomorphism, and \(\mu\) is a \(T\)-isomorphism. \textbf{Then
\(\alpha\) is cartesian if and only if \(\alpha'\) is cartesian}.

\textbf{Definition.}

An \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor \(F: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) is called
a \textbf{cartesian functor} if it transforms cartesian morphisms into
cartesian morphisms. We denote by \texttt{Hom̲\_cart(ℱ,𝒢)} the full
subcategory of \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℱ,𝒢)} formed by the cartesian
functors.

For example, regarding \(\mathcal{E}\) as a category over
\(\mathcal{E}\) by means of the identity functor, every morphism of
\(\mathcal{E}\) is cartesian. Thus a cartesian functor from
\(\mathcal{E}\) to \(\mathcal{F}\) is a section functor \(F:
\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{F}\) that transforms every morphism of
\(\mathcal{E}\) into a cartesian morphism. Such a functor is called a
\textbf{cartesian section} of \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\).

\textbf{Proposition.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A functor \(F: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) that is an
  \(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence is a cartesian functor.
\item
  Let \(F\), \(G\) be two \textbf{isomorphic} \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors
  \(\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\). If one is cartesian, then so is the
  other.
\item
  The composite of two cartesian functors
  \(\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) and \(\mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{H}\) is
  a cartesian functor.
\end{enumerate}

Assertion (3) is trivial from the definition; (2) follows from the
remark preceding VI.5.2; (1) follows easily from the definition and
criterion VI.4.2 (3). More precisely, a morphism \(\alpha\) in
\(\mathcal{F}\) is cartesian if and only if \(F(\alpha)\) is cartesian.

\textbf{Corollary.}

Let \(F: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) be an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence. Then for every category \(\mathcal{H}\)
over \(\mathcal{E}\), the corresponding functors \(G \mapsto G \circ F\)
and \(G \mapsto F \circ G\) induce equivalences of categories:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_cart(𝒢,ℋ) ≃ Hom̲\_cart(ℱ,ℋ),}
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_cart(ℋ,ℱ) ≃ Hom̲\_cart(ℋ,𝒢).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This follows in the usual way from criterion VI.4.2 (1) and from VI.5.3
(1), (2), (3).

One can specify that \textbf{the \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
\(G: \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{H}\) is cartesian if and only if \(G \circ
F\) is cartesian}, and likewise \textbf{an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
\(G: \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{F}\) is cartesian if and only if
\(F \circ G\) is cartesian}.

It follows from VI.5.4 (3) that, if one considers the subcategory
\(Cat^{cart}_{/}\mathcal{E}\) of \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\) whose objects
are the same as those of \(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}\) and whose morphisms are
the \textbf{cartesian} functors, then, as in VI.2, one has pairings

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_cart(ℱ,𝒢) × Hom̲\_cart(𝒢,ℋ) → Hom̲\_cart(ℱ,ℋ)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induced by those of VI.2. These pairings allow one to regard
\texttt{Hom̲\_cart(ℱ,𝒢)} as a functor in \(\mathcal{F}\) and
\(\mathcal{G}\), from the category
\texttt{(Cat\^{}cart\_/ℰ)°\ ×\ Cat\^{}cart\_/ℰ} to \texttt{Cat}. We
shall need this remark chiefly in the case
\(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{G}\).

\textbf{Definition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{E}\). We denote by

\[ Lim\leftarrow(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{E}) \]

the category of cartesian \(\mathcal{E}\)-functors
\(\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{F}\), i.e.~the cartesian sections of
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\).

By what has just been said, \(Lim\leftarrow(\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{E})\)
is a functor in \(\mathcal{F}\), from the category
\(Cat^{cart}_{/}\mathcal{E}\) to the category \texttt{Cat}.

We shall see below the relations between this operation
\(Lim\leftarrow\) and the notion of projective limit of categories, as
well as numerous examples.

\section{6. Fibered Categories and Prefibered Categories. Products and
Base Change in
Them}\label{fibered-categories-and-prefibered-categories.-products-and-base-change-in-them}

\textbf{Definition.}

A category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) is called a
\textbf{fibered category}, and the functor \(\mathcal{F} \to
\mathcal{E}\) is then said to be \textbf{fibrant}, if it satisfies the
two following axioms:

\textbf{Fib I.} For every morphism \(f: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\),
the inverse-image functor by \(f\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) exists.

\textbf{Fib II.} The composite of two cartesian morphisms is cartesian.

A category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) satisfying condition
\textbf{Fib I} is called a \textbf{prefibered category over
\(\mathcal{E}\)}.

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered, respectively prefibered, category over
\(\mathcal{E}\), a subcategory \(\mathcal{G}\) of \(\mathcal{F}\) is
called a \textbf{fibered subcategory}, respectively a \textbf{prefibered
subcategory}, if it is a fibered, respectively prefibered, category over
\(\mathcal{E}\) and, moreover, the inclusion functor is cartesian. If,
for example, \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \textbf{full} subcategory of
\(\mathcal{F}\), one sees that this means that, for every morphism
\(f: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\) and every
\(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{G}_{S})\), \(f*_{\mathcal{F}}(\xi)\) is
\(T\)-isomorphic to an object of \(\mathcal{G}_{T}\).

Another interesting case is the following. Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a
fibered category over \(\mathcal{E}\), and consider the subcategory
\(\mathcal{G}\) of \(\mathcal{F}\) with the same objects and whose
morphisms are the \textbf{cartesian} morphisms of \(\mathcal{F}\); in
particular the morphisms of \(\mathcal{G}_{S}\) are the isomorphisms of
\(\mathcal{F}_{S}\). One sees at once that this is indeed a fibered
subcategory of \(\mathcal{F}\), because in the bijection

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta',\eta) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta',\xi) \]

relative to a cartesian \(f\)-morphism \(\alpha\) in \(\mathcal{F}\),
the \(T\)-isomorphisms of the first member correspond to the cartesian
morphisms of the second. By definition, the cartesian sections
\(\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{F}\) then correspond bijectively to arbitrary
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors \(\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{G}\). However, note
that the natural functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/{-}\}(ℰ,𝒢) → Hom̲\_cart(ℰ,ℱ) = Lim←(ℱ/ℰ)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is faithful, but in general is not fully faithful, i.e.~is not an
isomorphism.

\textbf{Remarks.} Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over
\(\mathcal{E}\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  All morphisms of \(\mathcal{F}\) are cartesian.
\item
  \(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered category over \(\mathcal{E}\), and the
  \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) are groupoids, i.e.~every morphism in
  \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) is an isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}

One then says that \(\mathcal{F}\) is a category \textbf{fibered in
groupoids} over \(\mathcal{E}\).

These are the ones encountered especially in ``theory of moduli''. If
\(\mathcal{E}\) is a groupoid, one shows that conditions (1) and (2) are
also equivalent to the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\mathcal{F}\) is a groupoid, and the projection functor
  \(p: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{E}\) is transportable; cf. VI.4.4.
\end{enumerate}

For example, if \(\mathcal{E}\) and \(\mathcal{F}\) are groupoids such
that \(Ob(\mathcal{E})\) and \(Ob(\mathcal{F})\) are reduced to a point,
so that \(\mathcal{E}\) and \(\mathcal{F}\) are defined, up to
isomorphism, by groups \(E\) and \(F\), and the functor
\(p: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{E}\) is defined by a group homomorphism
\(p: F \to E\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) is fibered over \(\mathcal{E}\) if
and only if \(p\) is surjective, i.e.~if \(p\) defines an
\textbf{extension} of the group \(E\) by the group \(G = Ker p\).

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(F: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) be an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence. In order that \(\mathcal{F}\) be a fibered,
respectively prefibered, category over \(\mathcal{E}\), it is necessary
and sufficient that \(\mathcal{G}\) be so.

This follows easily from the definitions and from the remark made above
that a morphism \(\alpha\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) is cartesian if and only
if \(F(\alpha)\) is.

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}_{1}\), \(\mathcal{F}_{2}\) be two categories over
\(\mathcal{E}\), and let \(\alpha =
(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\) be a morphism in
\(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_{1} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{F}_{2}\).
Then \(\alpha\) is cartesian if and only if its components are
cartesian.

Indeed, let \(\xi_{i}\) be the target and \(\eta_{i}\) the source of
\(\alpha_{i}\), and let \(f: T \to S\) be the morphism of
\(\mathcal{E}\) such that \(\alpha_{1}\) and \(\alpha_{2}\) are
\(f\)-morphisms. For every \(\eta' = (\eta'_{1},\eta'_{2})\) in
\(\mathcal{F}_{T}\), one has a commutative diagram

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta',\eta) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta',\xi) \downarrow \downarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta'_{1},\eta_{1}) \times \operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta'_{2},\eta_{2}) \to
\operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta'_{1},\xi_{1}) \times \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta'_{2},\xi_{2}), \]

where the vertical arrows are bijections. Thus if one of the horizontal
arrows is a bijection, the same is true of the other. This already shows
that if \(\alpha_{1}\) and \(\alpha_{2}\) are cartesian, hence the
second horizontal arrow is bijective, then \(\alpha\) is cartesian. The
converse is seen by taking, in the diagram above,
\(\eta'_{i} = \eta_{i}\), whence
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta'_{i},\eta_{i}) \neq \emptyset\): first for
\(i = 2\), which proves that \(\alpha_{1}\) is cartesian, then for
\(i = 1\), which proves that \(\alpha_{2}\) is cartesian.

\textbf{Corollary.}

Let
\(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_{1} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{F}_{2}\),
and let \(F = (F_{1},F_{2})\) be an \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
\(\mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{F}\). Then \(F\) is cartesian if and only if
\(F_{1}\) and \(F_{2}\) are cartesian. One obtains in this way an
isomorphism of categories

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_cart(𝒢, ℱ₁ ×\_ℰ ℱ₂) ≃ Hom̲\_cart(𝒢,ℱ₁) × Hom̲\_cart(𝒢,ℱ₂),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and in particular, taking \(\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{E}\), an isomorphism
of categories

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lim←((ℱ₁ ×\_ℰ ℱ₂)/ℰ) ≃ Lim←(ℱ₁/ℰ) × Lim←(ℱ₂/ℰ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}_{1}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{2}\) be two fibered,
respectively prefibered, categories over \(\mathcal{E}\). Then their
fiber product
\(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_{1} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{F}_{2}\)
is a fibered, respectively prefibered, category over \(\mathcal{E}\).

These results moreover extend to the case of the fiber product of an
arbitrary family of categories over \(\mathcal{E}\).

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{E}\), with projection
functor \(p\), and let \(\lambda: \mathcal{E}' \to
\mathcal{E}\) be a functor. Regard
\(\mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}'\) as a
category over \(\mathcal{E}'\) by the projection functor
\(p' = p \times_{\mathcal{E}} id_{\mathcal{E}}'\). Let \(\alpha'\) be a
morphism of \(\mathcal{F}'\). Then \(\alpha'\) is a cartesian morphism
if and only if its image \(\alpha\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) is cartesian.

The proof is immediate and is left to the reader.

\textbf{Corollary.}

For every cartesian functor \(F: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) of
categories over \(\mathcal{E}\), the functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F′ = F ×\_ℰ ℰ′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

from \(\mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}'\) to
\(\mathcal{G}' = \mathcal{G} \times_{\mathcal{E}}
\mathcal{E}'\) is cartesian.

Consequently, the functor \texttt{Hom̲\_ℰ(ℱ,𝒢)\ →\ Hom̲\_ℰ′(ℱ′,𝒢′)}
considered in VI.3 induces a functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_cart(ℱ,𝒢) → Hom̲\_cart(ℱ′,𝒢′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In other words, for fixed \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\),
\textbf{one may regard}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom̲\_cart(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′, 𝒢 ×\_ℰ ℰ′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{as a functor in \(\mathcal{E}'\), from the category
\(Cat_{/}\mathcal{E}^{\circ}\) to \texttt{Cat}}. If \(\mathcal{F}\) and
\(\mathcal{G}\) are also allowed to vary, one finds a functor from the
category

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Cat\_/ℰ° × (Cat\^{}cart\_/ℰ)° × Cat\^{}cart\_/ℰ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

to \texttt{Cat}.

When one takes into account the isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_ℰ′(ℱ′,𝒢′) ≃ Hom\_ℰ(ℱ ×\_ℰ ℰ′,𝒢)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

considered in VI.3, the cartesian \(\mathcal{E}'\)-functors from
\(\mathcal{F}'\) to \(\mathcal{G}'\) correspond to the
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors
\(\mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{G}\) that
transform every morphism whose first projection is a cartesian morphism
of \(\mathcal{F}\) into a cartesian morphism of \(\mathcal{G}\). Taking
\(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{E}\), one finds, after a change of notation:

\textbf{Corollary.}

\(Lim\leftarrow(\mathcal{F}'/\mathcal{E}')\) is isomorphic to the full
subcategory of \texttt{Hom̲\_\{ℰ/-\}(ℰ′,ℱ)} formed by the
\(\mathcal{E}\)-functors \(\mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{F}\) that transform
arbitrary morphisms into cartesian morphisms. In particular, if
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered category and if \(\tilde{\mathcal{F}}\) is
the subcategory of \(\mathcal{F}\) whose morphisms are the cartesian
morphisms of \(\mathcal{F}\), then one has a bijection

\[ Ob Lim\leftarrow(\mathcal{F}'/\mathcal{E}') \simeq
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{E}/-}(\mathcal{E}',\tilde{\mathcal{F}}). \]

This makes precise the way in which the expression

\[ Lim\leftarrow((\mathcal{F} \times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}')/\mathcal{E}') \]

must be regarded as a functor in \(\mathcal{E}'\) and \(\mathcal{F}\),
from the category \texttt{Cat\_/ℰ°\ ×\ Cat\^{}cart\_/ℰ} to the category
\texttt{Cat}. Later we shall see a more complete functorial dependence
with respect to \(\mathcal{E}'\) when \(\mathcal{F}\) is required to be
a fibered category.

\textbf{Corollary.}

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered, respectively prefibered, category over
\(\mathcal{E}\), then \(\mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{F}
\times_{\mathcal{E}} \mathcal{E}'\) is a fibered, respectively
prefibered, category over \(\mathcal{E}'\).

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) be prefibered categories over
\(\mathcal{E}\), and let \(F\) be a cartesian \(\mathcal{E}\)-functor
from \(\mathcal{F}\) to \(\mathcal{G}\). In order that \(F\) be
faithful, respectively fully faithful, respectively an
\(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalence, it is necessary and sufficient that for
every \(S \in Ob(\mathcal{E})\), the induced functor

\[ F_{S}: \mathcal{F}_{S} \to \mathcal{G}_{S} \]

be faithful, respectively fully faithful, respectively an equivalence.

The proof is immediate from the definitions.

To finish this number, we give a few properties of fibered categories
using axiom \textbf{Fib II}.

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a prefibered category over \(\mathcal{E}\). In
order that \(\mathcal{F}\) be fibered, it is necessary and sufficient
that it satisfy the following condition:

\textbf{Fib II′.} Let \(\alpha: \eta \to \xi\) be a cartesian morphism
in \(\mathcal{F}\) over the morphism \(f: T \to S\) of \(\mathcal{E}\).
For every morphism \(g: U \to T\) in \(\mathcal{E}\), and every
\(\zeta \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{U})\), the map \(u
\mapsto \alpha \circ u\)

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{g}(\zeta,\eta) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{fg}(\zeta,\xi) \]

is bijective.

In other words, in a category \textbf{fibered} over \(\mathcal{E}\),
cartesian diagrams are characterized by a property a priori stronger
than the one in the definition, which is recovered by taking
\(g = id_{T}\) in the preceding statement.

\textbf{Corollary.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{E}\) and let
\(\alpha\) be a morphism in \(\mathcal{F}\). In order that \(\alpha\) be
an isomorphism, it is necessary that \(p(\alpha) = f\) be an isomorphism
and that \(\alpha\) be cartesian. The converse is true if
\(\mathcal{F}\) is fibered over \(\mathcal{E}\).

Indeed, if \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism then evidently so is
\(f = p(\alpha)\). For every \(\eta' \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{T})\), the map
\(u \mapsto \alpha \circ u\)

\[ \operatorname{Hom}(\eta',\eta) \to \operatorname{Hom}(\eta',\xi) \]

is bijective. Since \(f\) is an isomorphism, one sees at once that an
element of the first member is a \(T\)-morphism if and only if its image
in the second is an \(f\)-morphism. Thus one obtains a bijection

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta',\eta) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta',\xi), \]

which proves the first assertion. Conversely, suppose that \(f\) is an
isomorphism and that \(\alpha\) satisfies the condition stated in
\textbf{Fib II′}, which means, when \(\mathcal{F}\) is fibered over
\(\mathcal{E}\), that \(\alpha\) is cartesian. Then one sees at once
that for every \(\zeta \in Ob(\mathcal{F})\), the map
\(u \mapsto \alpha \circ u\) from \(\operatorname{Hom}(\zeta,\eta)\) to
\(\operatorname{Hom}(\zeta,\xi)\) is bijective, and hence \(\alpha\) is
an isomorphism.

\textbf{Corollary.}

Let \(\alpha: \eta \to \xi\) and \(\beta: \zeta \to \eta\) be two
composable morphisms in the category \(\mathcal{F}\) fibered over
\(\mathcal{E}\). If \(\alpha\) is cartesian, then \(\beta\) is cartesian
if and only if \(\alpha \beta\) is cartesian.

One uses the definition of cartesian morphisms in the strengthened form
VI.6.11.

\section{7. Categories Cloven over
ℰ}\label{categories-cloven-over-ux2130}

\textbf{Definition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a category over \(\mathcal{E}\). A
\textbf{cleavage} of \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) means a
function that attaches to every \(f \in Fl(\mathcal{E})\) an
inverse-image functor for \(f\) in \(\mathcal{F}\), denoted \(f*\). The
cleavage is said to be \textbf{normalized} if \(f = id_{S}\) implies
\(f* = id_{\mathcal{F}_{S}}\). A \textbf{cloven category}, respectively
a \textbf{normalized cloven category}, means a category \(\mathcal{F}\)
over \(\mathcal{E}\) endowed with a cleavage, respectively with a
normalized cleavage.

It is evident that \(\mathcal{F}\) admits a cleavage if and only if
\(\mathcal{F}\) is prefibered over \(\mathcal{E}\), and then
\(\mathcal{F}\) admits a normalized cleavage. The set of cleavages on
\(\mathcal{F}\) is in bijective correspondence with the set of subsets
\(K\) of \(Fl(\mathcal{F})\) satisfying the following conditions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The \(\alpha \in K\) are cartesian morphisms.
\item
  For every morphism \(f: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\) and every
  \(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{S})\), there exists a unique \(f\)-morphism
  in \(K\) with target \(\xi\).
\end{enumerate}

For the cleavage defined by \(K\) to be normalized, it is necessary and
sufficient that \(K\) also satisfy the condition:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The identity morphisms in \(\mathcal{F}\) belong to \(K\).
\end{enumerate}

The morphisms that are elements of \(K\) may be called the
\textbf{``transport morphisms''} for the cleavage in question.

The notion of isomorphism of cloven categories over \(\mathcal{E}\) is
clear. More generally, one can define morphisms of cloven
\(\mathcal{E}\)-categories as functors of \(\mathcal{E}\)-categories
\(\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{G}\) that send transport morphisms to
transport morphisms. These are, in particular, cartesian functors. In
this way the cloven categories over \(\mathcal{E}\) are the objects of a
category, the \textbf{category of cloven categories over
\(\mathcal{E}\)}. The reader may spell out the existence of products,
tied to the fact that if a category over \(\mathcal{E}\) is the product
of categories \(\mathcal{F}_{i}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), each endowed
with a cleavage, then \(\mathcal{F}\) is endowed with the corresponding
natural cleavage. We also leave to the reader the task of spelling out
the notion of base change in cloven categories.

We shall denote by \(\alpha_{f}(\xi)\) the canonical morphism

\[ \alpha_{f}(\xi): f*(\xi) \to \xi. \]

As was said, it is functorial in \(\xi\), i.e.~one has a functorial
homomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\_f: i\_T f* → i\_S,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where for every \(S \in Ob(\mathcal{E})\), \(i_{S}\) denotes the
inclusion functor

\[ i_{S}: \mathcal{F}_{S} \to \mathcal{F}. \]

Now consider morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f: T → S    and    g: U → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in \(\mathcal{E}\), and let \(\xi \in Ob(\mathcal{F}_{S})\). There then
exists a unique \(U\)-morphism

\[ c_{f,g}(\xi): g*f*(\xi) \to (fg)*(\xi) \]

making commutative

the diagram

\[ g*f*(\xi) --\alpha_{g}(f*(\xi))--> f*(\xi) | c_{f,g}(\xi) | \alpha_{f}(\xi) \downarrow \downarrow (fg)*(\xi)
--\alpha_{fg}(\xi)--> \xi, \]

by the definition of \((fg)*(\xi)\). For variable \(\xi\), this
homomorphism is functorial; that is, one has a homomorphism

\[ c_{f,g}: g*f* \to (fg)* \]

of functors \(\mathcal{F}_{S} \to \mathcal{F}_{U}\). Note at once:

\textbf{Proposition.}

In order that the cloven category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\)
be fibered, it is necessary and sufficient that the \(c_{f,g}\) be
isomorphisms.

It follows, taking \(f\) to be an isomorphism and \(g\) its inverse, and
considering the isomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) and \(c_{g,f}\):

\textbf{Corollary.}

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \textbf{fibered} cloven category over
\(\mathcal{E}\), then for every isomorphism \(f: T \to S\) in
\(\mathcal{E}\), \(f*\) is an equivalence of categories
\(\mathcal{F}_{S} \to \mathcal{F}_{T}\).

\textbf{Proposition.}

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a cloven category over \(\mathcal{E}\). One has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A)}
\NormalTok{  c\_\{f,id\_T\}(ξ) = α\_\{id\_T\}(f*(ξ)),}
\NormalTok{  c\_\{id\_S,f\}(ξ) = f*(α\_\{id\_S\}(ξ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B)  c\_\{f,gh\}(ξ) · c\_\{g,h\}(f*(ξ))}
\NormalTok{      = c\_\{fg,h\}(ξ) · h*(c\_\{f,g\}(ξ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In these formulas, \(f\), \(g\), \(h\) denote morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V → U → T → S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(\xi\) is an object of \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\).

In the case of a normalized cleavage, the first and second relations
take the simpler form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A′) c\_\{f,id\_T\} = id\_\{f*\},    c\_\{id\_S,f\} = id\_\{f*\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

As for the third, it is visualized by the commutativity of the diagram

\[
\begin{gathered}
h^*g^*f^*(\xi) \xrightarrow{c_{g,h}(f^*(\xi))} (gh)^*f^*(\xi) \\
{\scriptstyle h^*(c_{f,g}(\xi))}\ \downarrow \qquad\qquad
\downarrow\ {\scriptstyle c_{f,gh}(\xi)} \\
h^*(fg)^*(\xi) \xrightarrow{c_{fg,h}(\xi)} (fgh)^*(\xi).
\end{gathered}
\]

In the case of fibered categories, where the \(c_{f,g}\) are
isomorphisms, this commutativity may be expressed intuitively by saying
that \textbf{the successive use of isomorphisms of the form \(c_{f,g}\)
does not lead to ``contradictory identifications.''} One may also write
this formula without the argument \(\xi\), using the convolution product
of homomorphisms of functors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c\_\{fg,h\} ∘ (h* ∗ c\_\{f,g\}) = c\_\{f,gh\} ∘ (c\_\{g,h\} ∗ f*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proof of the first two formulas in VI.7.4 is trivial; let us sketch
that of the third. For this, consider, in addition to the square
\texttt{(D)}, the square of homomorphisms

\[ g*f*(\xi) --\alpha_{g}(f*(\xi))--> f*(\xi) | c_{f,g}(\xi) | \alpha_{f}(\xi) \downarrow \downarrow (fg)*(\xi)
--\alpha_{fg}(\xi)--> \xi, \]

which is commutative by definition of \(c_{f,g}(\xi)\). Consider the
diagram obtained by joining the vertices of \texttt{(D)} to the
corresponding vertices of this square by homomorphisms of the form
\(\alpha\):

\[ \alpha_{h}(g*f*(\xi)), \alpha_{gh}(f*(\xi)), \alpha_{h}((fg)*(\xi)), \alpha_{fgh}(\xi). \]

The four lateral faces of the cube so obtained are also commutative. For
the left face, this comes from the fact that the left column of
\texttt{(D)} is obtained from the left column of the preceding square by
applying \(h\), and that \(\alpha_{h}\) is a functorial homomorphism.
For the other three faces, this is nothing other than the definition of
the operations \(c\) on the remaining three sides of \texttt{(D)}. Thus
the five faces of the cube other than the upper face are commutative. It
follows that the two \texttt{(fgh)}-morphisms
\(h*g*f*(\xi) \to (fgh)*(\xi)\) defined by \texttt{(D)} have the same
composite with \(\alpha_{fgh}(\xi): (fgh)*(\xi) \to \xi\). Hence they
are equal by the definition of \((fgh)*\).

Let us confine ourselves, in what follows, to \textbf{normalized} cloven
categories. Such a category gives rise to the following objects:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A map \(S \mapsto \mathcal{F}_{S}\) from \(Ob(\mathcal{E})\) to
  \texttt{Cat}.
\item
  A map \(f \mapsto f*\), associating to every
  \(f \in Fl(\mathcal{E})\), with source \(T\) and target \(S\), a
  functor \(f*:
  \mathcal{F}_{S} \to \mathcal{F}_{T}\).
\item
  A map \((f,g) \mapsto c_{f,g}\), associating to every pair of arrows
  \((f,g)\) of \(\mathcal{E}\) a functorial homomorphism
  \(c_{f,g}: g*f* \to (fg)*\).
\end{enumerate}

Moreover, these data satisfy the conditions expressed in formulas A′)
and B) above. N.B. If one had not confined oneself to the case of a
normalized cleavage, one would have had to introduce an additional
object, namely a function \(S \mapsto
\alpha_{S}\) associating to every object \(S\) of \(\mathcal{E}\) a
functorial homomorphism \(\alpha_{S}: (id_{S})* \to
id_{\mathcal{F}_{S}}\); condition A′) would then be replaced by
condition A).

We shall now show how one can reconstruct, up to unique isomorphism, the
normalized cloven category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) from the
preceding objects.

\section{8. Cloven Category Defined by a Pseudofunctor ℰ° →
Cat}\label{cloven-category-defined-by-a-pseudofunctor-ux2130-cat}

For short, call a \textbf{pseudofunctor} from \(\mathcal{E}^{\circ}\) to
\texttt{Cat}, one should say a \textbf{normalized} pseudofunctor, a set
of data a), b), c) as above, satisfying conditions A′) and B). In the
preceding number we associated to a normalized cloven category over
\(\mathcal{E}\) a pseudofunctor \(\mathcal{E}^{\circ} \to Cat\). Here we
indicate the inverse construction. We shall leave to the reader the
verification of most of the details, as well as of the fact that these
constructions are indeed ``inverse'' to one another. More precisely, one
should regard the pseudofunctors \(\mathcal{E}^{\circ} \to Cat\) as the
objects of a new category, and show that our constructions provide
equivalences, quasi-inverse to one another, between this latter category
and the category of cloven categories over \(\mathcal{E}\) defined in
the preceding number.

Put

\[ \mathcal{F}^{\circ} = \coprod_{S\in Ob(\mathcal{E})} Ob(\mathcal{F}(S)), \]

the sum set of the sets \(Ob(\mathcal{F}(S))\). N.B. here we write
\(\mathcal{F}(S)\), and not \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\), for the value at the
object \(S\) of \(\mathcal{E}\) of the given pseudofunctor, to avoid
notational confusion later. We therefore have an evident map

\[ p^{\circ}: \mathcal{F}^{\circ} \to Ob(\mathcal{E}). \]

Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ξ̄ = (S,ξ),    η̄ = (T,η),    with ξ ∈ Ob(ℱ(S)), η ∈ Ob(ℱ(T)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be two elements of \(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}\), and let
\(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(T,S)\). Put

\[ h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}(T)}(\eta, f*(\xi)). \]

If in addition one has a morphism \(g: U \to T\) in \(\mathcal{E}\) and
\(\zeta \in Ob(\mathcal{F}(U))\), one defines a map, denoted
\((u,v) \mapsto u \circ v\),

\[ h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) \times h_{g}(\bar{\zeta},\bar{\eta}) \to h_{fg}(\bar{\zeta},\bar{\xi}), \]

i.e.~a map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{ℱ(T)\}(η, f*(ξ)) × Hom\_\{ℱ(U)\}(ζ, g*(η))}
\NormalTok{  → Hom\_\{ℱ(U)\}(ζ, (fg)*(ξ)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u ∘ v = c\_\{f,g\}(ξ) · g*(u) · v.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

That is, \(u \circ v\) is the composite of the sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ζ {-}{-}v{-}{-}\textgreater{} g*(η) {-}{-}g*(u){-}{-}\textgreater{} g*f*(ξ) {-}{-}c\_\{f,g\}(ξ){-}{-}\textgreater{} (fg)*(ξ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, put

\[ h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) = \coprod_{f\in \operatorname{Hom}(T,S)} h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}). \]

The preceding pairings define pairings

\[ h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) \times h(\bar{\zeta},\bar{\eta}) \to h(\bar{\zeta},\bar{\xi}), \]

while the definition of the \(h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\) gives an evident
map

\[ p_{\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}}: h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) \to \operatorname{Hom}(T,S). \]

This being said, one verifies the following points:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Composition between elements of the \(h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\) is
  \textbf{associative}.
\item
  For every \(\bar{\xi} = (S,\xi)\) in \(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}\), consider
  the identity element of
\end{enumerate}

\[ h_{id_{S}}(\bar{\xi},\bar{\xi}) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}(S)}(id_{S}*(\xi),\xi) =
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}(S)}(\xi,\xi), \]

and its image in \(h(\bar{\xi},\bar{\xi})\). This object is a
\textbf{left and right unit} for composition between elements of the
\(h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\).

This already shows that \textbf{one obtains a category} \(\mathcal{F}\)
by putting

\[ Ob(\mathcal{F}) = \mathcal{F}^{\circ}, Fl(\mathcal{F}) = \coprod_{\bar{\xi},\bar{\eta}\in \mathcal{F}^{\circ}}
h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}). \]

N.B. one cannot simply take \(Fl(\mathcal{F})\) to be the \textbf{union}
of the sets \(h(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\), since these latter sets are not
necessarily disjoint. Moreover:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The maps \(p^{\circ}: Ob(\mathcal{F}) \to Ob(\mathcal{E})\) and
  \(p_{1} = (p_{\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}}): Fl(\mathcal{F})
  \to Fl(\mathcal{E})\) define a \textbf{functor}
  \(p: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{E}\). In this way \(\mathcal{F}\)
  becomes a category over \(\mathcal{E}\); moreover, the evident map
  \(h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) \to
  \operatorname{Hom}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\) induces a
  \textbf{bijection}
\end{enumerate}

\[ h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}). \]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The evident maps
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ob(ℱ(S)) → ℱ° = Ob(ℱ),    Fl(ℱ(S)) → Fl(ℱ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the second is defined by the evident maps

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}(S)}(\xi,\xi') = h_{id_{S}}(\bar{\xi},\bar{\xi}') \to
\operatorname{Hom}(\bar{\xi},\bar{\xi}'), \]

define an \textbf{isomorphism}

\[ i_{S}: \mathcal{F}(S) \simeq \mathcal{F}_{S}. \]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  For every object \(\bar{\xi} = (S,\xi)\) of \(\mathcal{F}\), and every
  morphism \(f: T \to S\) of \(\mathcal{E}\), consider
\end{enumerate}

the element \(\bar{\eta} = (T,\eta)\) of \(\mathcal{F}_{T}\), with
\(\eta = f*(\xi)\), and the element \(\alpha_{f}(\xi)\) of
\(\operatorname{Hom}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\), image of \(id_{f*(\xi)}\)
by the morphism

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}(T)}(f*(\xi),f*(\xi)) = h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}) \to
\operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi}). \]

\textbf{This element is cartesian, and it is the identity of
\(\bar{\xi}\) if \(f = id_{S}\)}. In other words, the set of the
\(\alpha_{f}(\xi)\) defines a \textbf{normalized cleavage of
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\)}. Moreover, by construction, one
has commutativity in the diagram of functors

\[ \mathcal{F}(S) --f*--> \mathcal{F}(T) | i_{S} | i_{T} \downarrow \downarrow \mathcal{F}_{S} --f*_{\mathcal{F}}->
\mathcal{F}_{T}, \]

where \(f*_{\mathcal{F}}\) is the inverse-image functor by \(f\),
relative to the cleavage considered on \(\mathcal{F}\). Finally:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The homomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) given with the pseudofunctor are
  transformed, by the isomorphisms \(i_{S}\), into the functorial
  homomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) associated with the cleavage of
  \(\mathcal{F}\).
\end{enumerate}

We restrict ourselves to giving the verification of 1), which is, if
anything, less trivial than the others. It suffices to prove
associativity of composition between objects of sets of the form
\(h_{f}(\bar{\eta},\bar{\xi})\). Thus consider in \(\mathcal{E}\)
morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S ←\^{}f T ←\^{}g U ←\^{}h V}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and objects

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ξ, η, ζ, τ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in \(\mathcal{F}(S)\), \(\mathcal{F}(T)\), \(\mathcal{F}(U)\),
\(\mathcal{F}(V)\), and finally elements

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u ∈ h\_f(η̄,ξ̄) = Hom\_\{ℱ(T)\}(η, f*(ξ)),}
\NormalTok{v ∈ h\_g(ζ̄,η̄) = Hom\_\{ℱ(U)\}(ζ, g*(η)),}
\NormalTok{w ∈ h\_h(τ̄,ζ̄) = Hom\_\{ℱ(V)\}(τ, h*(ζ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We want to prove the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u ∘ v) ∘ w = u ∘ (v ∘ w),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is an equality in
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{F}(V)}(\tau,(fgh)*(\xi))\). By the
definitions, the two members of this equality are obtained by
composition along the upper and lower contours of the diagram below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{τ {-}{-}w{-}{-}\textgreater{} h*(ζ) {-}{-}h*(v){-}{-}\textgreater{} h*g*(η) {-}{-}h*g*(u){-}{-}\textgreater{} h*g*f*(ξ) {-}{-}h*(c\_\{f,g\}(ξ)){-}{-}\textgreater{} h*(fg)*(ξ)}
\NormalTok{ \textbackslash{}\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ v∘w \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_/       | c\_\{g,h\}(f*(ξ))              | c\_\{fg,h\}(ξ)}
\NormalTok{                         ↓                              ↓                             ↓}
\NormalTok{                  (gh)*(η) {-}{-}(gh)*(u){-}{-}\textgreater{}        (gh)*f*(ξ) {-}{-}c\_\{f,gh\}(ξ){-}{-}\textgreater{}       (fgh)*(ξ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The middle square is commutative because \(c_{g,h}\) is a functorial
homomorphism, and the square on the right is commutative by condition B)
for a pseudofunctor. This gives the asserted result.

Of course, it remains to specify, when the pseudofunctor considered
already comes from a normalized cloven category \(\mathcal{F}'\) over
\(\mathcal{E}\), how one obtains a natural isomorphism between
\(\mathcal{F}'\) and \(\mathcal{F}\). We leave the details to the
reader.

We likewise leave to the reader the interpretation, in terms of
pseudofunctors, of the notion of inverse image of a cloven category
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) by a base-change functor
\(\mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E}\).

\section{9. Example: Cloven Category Defined by a Functor ℰ° → Cat;
Split Categories over
ℰ}\label{example-cloven-category-defined-by-a-functor-ux2130-cat-split-categories-over-ux2130}

Suppose one has a functor

\[ \phi: \mathcal{E}^{\circ} \to Cat. \]

It then defines a pseudofunctor by putting

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℱ(S) = φ(S),    f* = φ(f),    c\_\{f,g\} = id\_\{(fg)*\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Thus the construction of the preceding number gives us a category
\(\mathcal{F}\) cloven over \(\mathcal{E}\), said to be associated with
the functor \(\phi\). For a cloven category over \(\mathcal{E}\) to be
isomorphic to a cloven category defined by a functor
\(\phi: \mathcal{E}^{\circ} \to Cat\), it is manifestly necessary and
sufficient that it satisfy the conditions

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(fg)* = g*f*,    c\_\{f,g\} = id\_\{(fg)*\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In terms of the set \(K\) of transport morphisms, this also simply means
that \textbf{the composite of two transport morphisms is a transport
morphism}. A cleavage of a category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\)
satisfying the preceding condition is called a \textbf{splitting} of
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), and a category \(\mathcal{F}\)
over \(\mathcal{E}\) endowed with a splitting is called a \textbf{split
category over \(\mathcal{E}\)}. It is therefore a special case of the
notion of cloven category. The category of split categories over
\(\mathcal{E}\) is therefore equivalent to \texttt{Hom̲(ℰ°,Cat)}. Note
that a split category over \(\mathcal{E}\) is a fortiori a cloven
category over \(\mathcal{E}\).

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered category over \(\mathcal{E}\), there
does not always exist a splitting on \(\mathcal{F}\). Suppose for
example that \(Ob(\mathcal{E})\) and \(Ob(\mathcal{F})\) are reduced to
one element, and that the set of endomorphisms of that element is a
group \(E\), respectively \(F\), so that the projection functor \(p\) is
given by a group homomorphism \(p: F \to E\), surjective since \(p\) is
fibrant. One verifies at once that the set of cleavages of
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) is in bijective correspondence with
the set of maps \(s: E \to F\) such that \(ps =
id_{E}\), i.e.~the set of ``systems of representatives'' for the classes
modulo the subgroup \(G\) that is the kernel of the surjective
homomorphism \(p: F \to E\). A cleavage is a splitting if and only if
\(s\) is a group homomorphism. To say that a splitting exists therefore
means that the group extension \(F\) of \(E\) by \(G\) is trivial, which
is expressed, when \(G\) is commutative, by the vanishing of a certain
cohomology class in \(H^{2}(E,G)\), where \(G\) is regarded as a group
on which \(E\) operates.

Suppose, however, that \(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered category over
\(\mathcal{E}\) such that the

\(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) are \textbf{rigid} categories, i.e.~the automorphism
group of every object of \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) is reduced to the identity.
It is then easy to prove that \(\mathcal{F}\) admits a splitting over
\(\mathcal{E}\). Indeed, one first observes that the question of
existence of a splitting is not changed if \(\mathcal{F}\) is replaced
by an \(\mathcal{E}\)-equivalent category. This reduces us in the
present case to the case where the \(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) are rigid
\textbf{and reduced} categories, i.e.~two isomorphic objects in
\(\mathcal{F}_{S}\) are identical. But if \(G\) is a rigid and reduced
category, every isomorphism between two functors \(H \to G\), where
\(H\) is any category, is an identity. It follows that if
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a fibered category over \(\mathcal{E}\) whose fiber
categories are rigid and reduced, then there exists a \textbf{unique}
cleavage of \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), which is necessarily a
splitting. Thus \(\mathcal{F}\) is isomorphic to the category defined by
a functor \(\phi: \mathcal{E}^{\circ} \to Cat\) such that the
\(\phi(S)\) are rigid and discrete categories, and the functor \(\phi\)
is defined up to isomorphism.

\section{10. Co-Fibered Categories, Bi-Fibered
Categories}\label{co-fibered-categories-bi-fibered-categories}

Consider a category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\), with
projection functor

\[ p: \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{E}. \]

It defines a category \(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}\) over
\(\mathcal{E}^{\circ}\) by the projection functor

\[ p^{\circ}: \mathcal{F}^{\circ} \to \mathcal{E}^{\circ}. \]

A morphism \(\alpha: \eta \to \xi\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) is said to be
\textbf{co-cartesian} if it is a cartesian morphism for
\(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}\) over \(\mathcal{E}^{\circ}\). Spelling this out,
one sees that it means that for every object \(\xi'\) of
\(\mathcal{F}_{S}\), the map \(u \mapsto u \circ \alpha\)

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(\xi,\xi') \to \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta,\xi') \]

is bijective. One then also says that \((\xi,\alpha)\) is a
\textbf{direct image} of \(\eta\) by \(f\), in the category
\(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\). If it exists for every \(\eta\) in
\(\mathcal{F}_{T}\), one says that the direct-image functor by \(f\)
exists; once it has been chosen, this functor is denoted

\[ f*_{\mathcal{F}} or f_{*}. \]

It is therefore defined by an isomorphism of bifunctors on
\(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}_{T} \times \mathcal{F}_{S}\):

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(f_{*}(\eta),\xi) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{f}(\eta,\xi). \]

Thus, if \(f_{*}\) exists, then for \(f*\) to exist it is necessary and
sufficient that \(f_{*}\) admit an adjoint functor, i.e.~that there
exist a functor \(f*: \mathcal{F}_{S} \to \mathcal{F}_{T}\) and an
isomorphism of bifunctors

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(f_{*}(\eta),\xi) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{T}(\eta,f*(\xi)). \]

Let \(g: U \to T\) be another morphism in \(\mathcal{E}\), and suppose
that the inverse and direct images by \(f\), \(g\), and \texttt{fg}
exist. Consider then the functorial homomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c\^{}\{f,g\}: f\_* g\_* ← (fg)\_*,}
\NormalTok{c\_\{f,g\}: g* f* → (fg)*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One observes that, if \(f_{*} g_{*}\) and \(g* f*\) are regarded as a
pair of adjoint functors, and likewise \((fg)_{*}\) and \((fg)*\), then
the two preceding homomorphisms are adjoint to one another. Thus one is
an isomorphism if and only if the other is. In particular:

\textbf{Proposition.}

Suppose that the category \(\mathcal{F}\) over \(\mathcal{E}\) is
prefibered and co-prefibered. In order that it be fibered, it is
necessary and sufficient that it be co-fibered.

Of course, \(\mathcal{F}\) is said to be co-prefibered, respectively
co-fibered, over \(\mathcal{E}\) if \(\mathcal{F}^{\circ}\) is
prefibered, respectively fibered, over \(\mathcal{E}\). We shall say
that \(\mathcal{F}\) is \textbf{bi-fibered} over \(\mathcal{E}\) if it
is both fibered and co-fibered over \(\mathcal{E}\).

\section{11. Various Examples}\label{various-examples}

\subsection{a) Categories of Arrows of
ℰ}\label{a-categories-of-arrows-of-ux2130}

Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a category. Denote by \(\Delta^{1}\) the category
associated with the totally ordered set with two elements
\texttt{{[}0,1{]}}. It therefore has two objects \texttt{0} and
\texttt{1}, and besides the two identity morphisms one arrow
\texttt{(0,1)} with source \texttt{0} and target \texttt{1}. Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ar(ℰ) = Hom̲(Δ¹,ℰ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is called the \textbf{category of arrows of} \(\mathcal{E}\). The
object \texttt{1} of \(\Delta^{1}\) defines a canonical functor, called
the \textbf{target functor}

\[ Ar(\mathcal{E}) \to \mathcal{E} \]

the functor defined by the object \texttt{0} of \(\Delta^{1}\) being
called the \textbf{source functor}. For every object \(S\) of
\(\mathcal{E}\), the fiber category \(Ar(\mathcal{E})_{S}\) is
canonically isomorphic to the category \(\mathcal{E}_{/}S\) of objects
of \(\mathcal{E}\) over \(S\).

Consider a morphism \(f: T \to S\) in \(\mathcal{E}\). To it there
corresponds a canonical functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_*: ℰ\_/T = ℱ\_T → ℰ\_/S = ℱ\_S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and a functorial isomorphism
